statement: How many four-digit numbers have at least one pair of equal digits standing next to each other, such as 3557 or 1000?

choices.misconception: I counted the numbers with no two equal neighbouring digits, which is the opposite of what was asked.
I subtracted 6561 from 10000, but there are only 9000 four-digit numbers.
I thought no equal neighbours meant all four digits different, so I subtracted $9 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 4536$ from 9000.
I allowed 10 choices for the first digit of a number with no equal neighbours, getting 7290 instead of 6561.

hints: It is easier to count the numbers that do not have this property.
Complementary counting: count the four-digit numbers in which every digit differs from the one before it, then subtract from the total number of four-digit numbers.
The first digit has 9 choices (not 0). Every later digit also has 9 choices: anything except the digit just before it.

solutions.reliable: There are 9000 four-digit numbers. Count those with no two equal neighbours: the first digit has 9 choices (1 to 9), and each of the next three digits can be any of the 10 digits except the one just before it, so 9 choices each. That gives $9^4 = 6561$. So $9000 - 6561 = 2439$ numbers have a pair of equal neighbours. The transferable idea: 'at least one' is usually counted as the total minus 'none'.

whyOnTest: An 'at least one' condition is a signal for complementary counting, and the traps are using the wrong total or the wrong complement.
